en: The *Zhiguan Mingjing* (Clarifying Stillness of Stopping and Contemplation), spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty and recorded by his disciple Guanding,
was unheard of in previous generations. Zhizhe [lived during] the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Great Sui.
On the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month,
at Yique Spring Monastery in Jingzhou,
he expounded the teachings throughout the summer retreat, showering compassion twice daily.
Although his eloquence was inexhaustible, as soon as he reached the realm of direct perception,
the turning of the Wheel of Dharma ceased and its subsequent portions were not proclaimed.
Nevertheless, by drawing from the stream to seek the source and following the fragrance to investigate the root, [one may understand it].

At first at the Deer Park, and later at Vulture Peak.
Later, at the Crane Forest (Kūṭāgāraśālā),
the Dharma was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
Kāśyapa divided the relics into eight portions and convened the council to compile the Tripiṭaka.
The Dharma was entrusted to Ānanda.
Ānanda entered the *vāyu-samādhi* by the river and divided his body into four parts.
The Dharma was then entrusted to Śāṇakavāsin.
He practiced the "Two Hands of Amṛta" and manifested five hundred dharma-gates.
He entrusted the Dharma to Guptaka;
Guptaka mostly remained a layman yet attained the third fruit of the path.
By receiving the precepts, one attains the four fruits;
the Dharma was entrusted to Kātyāyana;
and many ascended the altar to attain the first fruit.
Through three *karmavācanās*, one attains the four fruits.
The Dharma was entrusted to Micaka;
Micaka entrusted it to Buddhānandi.
The Buddha entrusted [the Dharma] to Maitreya;
Maitreya bestowed the Three Refuges upon King Śatānīka and subdued the calculators.
He entrusted the Dharma to the Bhikṣu Pārśva.
The bhikṣu emerged from the womb with white hair; his hands emitted light as he took up the scriptures.
He entrusted the Dharma to Pūrṇaśa, whose debate triumphed over Aśvaghoṣa.
Having shaved his hair, he became a disciple.
As he sang the praises of Ratthapala,
the sound of his song expounded upon impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.
Those who heard him awakened to the Way.
He transmitted the Dharma to Vīra.
Vīra composed the *Nairātmya-śāstra* (Treatise on Non-Self).
The treatise was directed toward the place where wrong views were extinguished.
The Dharma was entrusted to Nāgārjuna;
through him, the birth-body became the Dharma-body.
The Dharma was entrusted to Devadatta;
he excavated the divine eye and bestowed it upon the ten thousand who possessed only physical eyes.
The Dharma was entrusted to Rāhula.
The name of the ghost who subdued the non-Buddhists was written as Lashi;
the Dharma was entrusted to Saṃkhya Nandi,
who spoke a verse to test the Arhat.
The Dharma was entrusted to Saṃghayaśas.
While traveling by sea, Yaśas saw a city and spoke a verse.
The Dharma was then entrusted to Kumārabhadra.
Dha saw ten thousand cavalry and recorded the colors of their horses;
De obtained people's names and distinguished their garments;
the Dharma was entrusted to Śāṇakavāsin.

Dharmamānuṣa divided the Ganges into two parts;
he himself transformed one part.
The Dharma was entrusted to Kṣemaka;
he entrusted it to Siṃha.
Siṃha was killed by King Damila, who slew him with a sword from which milk flowed.
Regarding the persons of the Dharma-treasury transmission:
beginning with Kāśyapa and ending with Siṃha, there were twenty-three individuals.
Madhyāntika and Śāṇakavāsin received [the transmission] at the same time.
Thus, there are twenty-four individuals;
all were recorded by the golden mouth [of the Buddha],
and all are sages capable of bringing great benefit.

he attained perfect realization in a single moment through ninety days of constant sitting;
the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were then clearly and penetratingly revealed to him.

Tiantai transmitted from Nanyue three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*:
first, the gradual; second, the non-gradual (or indeterminate).
The three— Perfect, Sudden,
and [Gradual]— are all Mahāyāna;
they all take true reality as their object and are equally termed "calm abiding" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā).
The gradual [approach] is shallow at first and deep later, like the rungs of a ladder;
the indeterminate [approach] has no fixed sequence, as they alternate with one another,
like a diamond jewel placed in the midst of the sun.
In the Perfect and Sudden teaching, the beginning and the end are non-dual, like one who possesses supernatural powers soaring through the air.
For those of the three capacities, three Dharma-gates are taught, illustrated by three metaphors.

To explain further:
from the very beginning, one also comes to know the true nature (dharmatā).
While the true nature is difficult to comprehend, it is easy to practice through gradual stages.
First, one cultivates taking refuge and observing the precepts to turn away from heterodoxy and incline toward the correct path;
by extinguishing fire, blood, and the blade, one reaches the three wholesome realms.
Next, one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to cease the net of sensual distraction.
One masters the paths of the form and formless realms;
next, one cultivates the untainted (*anāsrava*) tranquility (*śamatha*) to transcend the prison of the three realms and master the path to nirvāṇa.
Next, one cultivates the cessation of compassion until it reaches self-realization and attains the Bodhisattva path;
thereafter, one cultivates the cessation of the true mark to eliminate the extremes of duality.
One attains the eternally abiding Way;
this constitutes the characteristic of gradual cessation and contemplation, being shallow at first and deepening thereafter.
Regarding "indeterminate":
there are no distinct stages to distinguish between the preceding gradual and the subsequent sudden,
nor between what precedes and what follows.
They are mutually shallow and mutually deep;
whether in terms of phenomena or principle,

or, the cessation of discursive observation is designated as "calming," while the illumination of that cessation is designated as "insight."
Therefore, it is called "indeterminate samatha-vipaśyanā. A doubter asks:

It is only from the perspective of the majority that they are said to be different;
the meaning is that all noble ones (āryas) are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
This is precisely what it signifies.
As for the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]:
from the very beginning, one takes the true reality as the object; the created realm is itself the Middle Way, wherein nothing is not real.
One binds the conditions to the Dharma-realm; in a single thought-moment, one is the Dharma-realm.
A single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way;
so it is with one's own realm, the Buddha-realm, and the realm of sentient beings.
The aggregates and sense bases are all suchness, and there is no suffering to be abandoned.
Ignorance and the afflictions are themselves bodhi; there is no accumulation to be severed.
Extremes and deviance are all the Middle Way; there is no path to be cultivated.
Birth and death are themselves nirvana; there is no cessation to be realized.
Because there is no suffering and no origin, there is no mundane world.
Because there is no path and no cessation, there is no supramundane world.
It is the single, uniform, true reality.
Apart from the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), there are no other dharmas.
The quiescence of the dharma-nature (dharmatā) is called śamatha;
its constant illumination while remaining quiescent is called vipaśyanā.
Although it is said that there is neither duality nor distinction between the beginning and the end,

Now, based on the sūtras, I shall further clarify the Perfect and Sudden [teaching].
As the Bodhisattvas Śrīgarbha and Bhadramukha, who have thoroughly realized the profound and wondrous virtue, said:
"When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment within saṃsāra..."
Seeking enlightenment with single-minded resolve, they are firm and immovable.
The merit of even a single thought of theirs is so profound and vast that it has no limit;
though a Tathāgata were to explain it in detail for an entire kalpa, he could not exhaust it.
This Bodhisattva, hearing the perfect Dharma,
gives rise to perfect faith and establishes perfect practice.
Abiding in the stage of perfection,
he adorns himself with perfect virtues and establishes sentient beings through perfect powers and functions.
What is meant by hearing the perfect Dharma?
It is hearing that birth-and-death is itself the Dharmakāya,
and that afflictions are themselves Prajñā.
Karmic bondage is itself liberation.
Although there are three names, there are not three essences;
although it is a single essence, three names are established.
These three are in fact a single characteristic;
in reality, there is no difference between them.
The Dharma-body is ultimate, and both Prajñā and liberation are likewise ultimate.
When prajñā is pure, all else is also pure;
when liberation is sovereign, all else is also sovereign;
and it is likewise for hearing all dharmas.
All fully possess the Buddha-dharma without any deficiency;
this is called hearing the perfect Dharma.
What is perfect faith?
One has faith that all phenomena are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle;
yet they are neither one, two, nor three, while being one, two, and three.
That they are not one, two, or three is the negation of one, two, and three.
Yet, one, two, and three are the illumination of one, two, and three;
with neither obstruction nor illumination, all are ultimately pure and sovereign.
Hearing the profound, one is not terrified; hearing the vast, one does not doubt.
To hear that which is neither deep nor vast and yet possess courage in one's resolve—
this is called perfect faith.
What is perfect practice?
One single-mindedly and exclusively seeks unsurpassed bodhi;
thus, while at the periphery, one is already at the center, with no further inclinations elsewhere.
One practices the three truths in their perfect unity, neither stilled by the infinite nor moved by the finite.
Without moving and without quiescence, one enters directly into the Middle Way;
this is called perfect practice (*paripūrṇa-caryā*).
How does one enter the stage of perfection?
Upon entering the first stage, one stage encompasses all stages;
all are ultimate, all are pure, and all are sovereign.
This is called the Perfect Stage.
What is the adornment of perfect mastery?
That sūtra explains the characteristics of mastery in detail;

"How many are horizontal and vertical, and how many are neither horizontal nor vertical?

The first eight chapters are both conventional and ultimate.

From the general intent to the arousal of the teaching is the head;
from the skillful means to the retribution of the fruit is the feet.
The ultimate goal is common to both the [teaching on] the eyes and feet and to the Great Meaning of Perfect Contemplation; however,
the retribution and the arousal of the teaching are not common.

Question:

Since the manifest and the secret have already been distinguished,

Why does the listener perform contemplation?

Question:

This is the meditation on the indeterminate.

Answer: The intention of the Hīnayāna is not that the three [stages] are the characteristics of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Question:
The Hīnayāna is also taught by the Buddha;

Question:
Regarding the demonstration of the three phrases:

If it is not a gateway, [then...]

Answer: All phenomena are, in their very nature, the true reality (dharmatā).
Sentient beings mostly possess inverted views and few possess non-inverted views.
To demonstrate this through words:

The letter is its gateway, for through the gateway one attains the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

it is the gateway, it is not the gateway, and it is neither not the gateway nor not-not the gateway.

The intention being lax makes it difficult to perceive; now, I shall summarize it into five points:
namely, generating the great resolve and cultivating the great practice.
One experiences great fruition,
tears asunder the great net,
and returns to the Great Abode.
What is the arousal of the great mind?
Sentient beings are mired in delusion and do not realize it themselves;
one exhorts them to awaken, seeking the higher path while transforming those below.

What is meant by "tearing asunder the great net"?
Various sūtras and śāstras open the eyes of people,

Hearing of snow, one calls it cold; hearing of cranes, one calls them moving.
Now, having integrated the sutras and śāstras to untie the knots and emerge from the cage, how does one return to the Great Abode?
Dharmas have no beginning or end; dharmas have no obstruction or penetration.

Regarding the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*), there are further three [aspects].
First, the words:
Next, the non-[Bodhi] is excluded;

"Bodhi" is a term from the Indic language; in this land, it is called "the Way."
"Citta" is a term from the Indic language; in this dialect [of Chinese], it refers to the "mind," specifically the mind that cogitates and knows.

If one’s mind, in every thought-moment, is exclusively preoccupied with greed, hatred, and delusion.
They are restrained yet do not return; they are pulled out yet do not emerge.
Day by day they increase and month by month they worsen, giving rise to the ten grave evils of the highest degree, such as those who are pañcāśatikas.
This arousal of the mind for hell leads one onto the path of fiery trails.
If that mind, moment by moment, desires many followers—
as the ocean swallows rivers or as fire consumes fuel— [it leads to such a fate].
When one gives rise to the ten unwholesome actions of medium grade—
such as Devadatta’s instigation of the multitude—
one generates the mind of an animal and proceeds upon the path of bloodshed.
If their minds, in every thought-moment, desire to gain renown throughout the four quarters and the eight directions, being praised and admired from afar,
yet they lack internal, genuine virtue while falsely comparing themselves to the worthy and the sages,
they give rise to the minor grade of the ten unwholesome actions.
As for Mākaṇḍika, he harbored a demonic mind and traveled along the path of the executioners;
in every thought-moment, his mind constantly desired to surpass others and could not tolerate those who were inferior.
Contemptuous of others while cherishing oneself, like an eagle soaring high and looking down,
they outwardly proclaim benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and sincerity; yet,
giving rise to only inferior wholesome thoughts, they practice the path of the asuras.
If their mind, in every thought-moment, delights in worldly pleasures,
settling its foul body and gladdening its deluded mind,
they give rise to a middling degree of wholesome mind and proceed through the human realm.
If one’s mind, in every thought-moment, recognizes that the sufferings of the three evil realms are many,
that human existence is a mixture of suffering and pleasure,
and that the heavens consist of pure bliss.
For the sake of celestial bliss, one restrains the six sense faculties so that they do not issue forth toward the six sense objects nor enter into them;
this superior grade of virtuous mind leads to rebirth in the heavenly realms.
If, however, one’s mind in every thought-moment desires great power and majesty, [it leads elsewhere].
Whatever actions he performs with body, speech, or mind, all follow his will.
This is the arising of the mind of a lord of the desire realm who follows the path of Māra.
If his mind, moment by moment, desires to obtain sharp wisdom, eloquence, brilliance, high talent, courage, and sagacity, [he shall attain them].
He clearly perceives the six directions and the ten realms, and all gaze toward him with reverence.
This is the arousal of worldly wisdom; his mind and conduct follow the path of the Nirgranthas.
If his mind, in every thought-moment, finds that the pleasures of the five sensory objects and the six desires are but minor obscurations, [he shall transcend them].
The bliss of the third dhyāna is like a spring from within a rock; its joy is profound within.
This gives rise to the Brahma-mind and leads one to practice the paths of the form and formless realms.
If one’s mind, in every thought-moment, knows the cyclical turning of good and evil, [one shall attain liberation].
Ordinary persons are addicted to these and are censured by the noble ones.
The destruction of evil arises from pure wisdom;
pure wisdom arises from pure meditative concentration.
Regarding pure meditation, one values these three dharmas—pure precepts and so forth—as much as one craves food or thirst for water.
This gives rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava) mind that practices the paths of the two vehicles;

This is precisely the meaning of falling into the animal realm due to a mind devoid of shame and remorse. Alternatively,

Either this mind arises first,

it is like an elephant, a fish, and the wind all together turbidifying the water of a pond.
The elephant represents the external; the fish represents the internal;

Furthermore, the elephant represents all things that do not arise from the outside.
The fish is a metaphor for internal contemplation that is weak and moved by the two extremes.
The wind is a metaphor for the external and internal being combined, defiled, turbid, and intermingled.
Furthermore, these nine types are like birth and death, as when a silkworm binds itself.
The latter one refers to *nirvāṇa*, which is like a deer leaping alone;

Because both [the former and the latter] are "neither," they are excluded together.
The first nine are mundane, being neither unmoving nor emerging;
the latter one, although it emerges, lacks great compassion—thus they are distinguished as neither-and-not.
They are both conditioned and unconditioned, and both with outflows and without outflows.
The various dharma-gates, such as good and evil, defilement and purity, bondage and liberation,
and the ultimate and conventional truths, are likewise so. Furthermore,

The latter one is not the Truth of Suffering;
although it is not the Truth of Suffering, because it is crooked, clumsy, ash-like, and proximate, both are excluded by this double negation.
Next, conditioned and out-flowing phenomena are categorized under the Truth of Origination.
The latter one is not the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Although it is not the Truth of Origination, it is also excluded by being "crooked," "near," "ash-like," and "clumsy"—thus it is distinguished by being a double negation.
Next, regarding good and evil, and defilement and purity, these are categorized according to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
The last one is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Although it is the Truth of the Path, it is also distinguished as before.
Next, bondage and liberation are distinguished in terms of the ultimate and conventional truths regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Although the latter one is indeed the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), it is also distinguished as before. If one grasps this meaning,
then throughout all sense organs and objects, the three karmas, and the four modes of conduct, whenever the mind arises or a thought moves, [one remains in this state].
One should observe all things in this way so that no turbid states of mind arise;

It is like a person with clear vision who is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths.

This is further concluded by means of the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*),

○ Manifesting this further divides it into three parts.
First, the Four Noble Truths;
next, the Four Great Vows;
and finally, the Six Identities.
The names and characteristics of the Four Noble Truths appear in the "Chapter on Holy Practice" (*Āryacaryā*) of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

They are: arising-and-ceasing (*utpādavyaya*), non-arising-and-non-ceasing (*anutpādāvyaya*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*). "Arising-and-ceasing" refers to suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), which are the causes and effects of the world.
The Path and Cessation transcend the world as cause and effect;
Suffering involves the shifting of the three characteristics,
while Origination involves the movement of the four minds.
The Path is easily usurped by its opposites;
cessation involves the extinction of existence and the return to non-existence.
Thus, both the mundane and the supramundane are subject to transformation and change.
Therefore, they are called the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing.
As for "non-arising":
suffering is without oppression, and all things are empty.
How could emptiness be able to dispel emptiness?
Form itself is emptiness;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Therefore, there is no characteristic of oppression.
As for the absence of the characteristic of aggregation in the arising [of phenomena],
both cause and effect are empty.
How could there be a cause that is empty uniting with a fruit that is empty?
This applies likewise to all instances of greed, hatred, and delusion.
In the Path, there is no duality of characteristics; there is neither that which can cure nor that which is cured.
Since even emptiness does not possess a single [dharma], how could there be two?
Dharmas are fundamentally non-arising; now they are non-ceasing.
Because they neither arise nor cease, they are called the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising.
Regarding "immeasurable":
one discriminates and calculates that suffering has immeasurable aspects;
that is to say, even within a single dharma-realm, suffering is already manifold.
How much more so for the ten dharma realms, which are manifold and diverse;
these cannot be known or seen by the wisdom or the eyes of the two vehicles,
but can only be clearly understood by bodhisattvas.
This refers to the various and manifold distinctions within the hells—
being pierced, flayed, sliced, burned, boiled, and hacked—
which are still further beyond measure and calculation.
How much more so for the various forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses of other realms;
how could the sands of the Ganges, the oceans, or the drops of water ever be exhausted?
Therefore, this is not within the knowledge and vision of the two vehicles.
Only the Bodhisattva’s eye of wisdom can penetrate this.
Furthermore, it accumulates immeasurable characteristics;
that is to say, the various minds and various karmas of body and speech accumulated through greed, hatred, and delusion in their manifold forms.
When the body is bent, the shadow is slanted; when the voice is clamorous, the resonance is turbid.
The Bodhisattva perceives these without error.
Furthermore, it is said that there are immeasurable characteristics.

This refers to the analytical discernment of the essence through skillful and unskillful means, the crooked and the straight, the long and the short, and the provisional and the ultimate; it is the bodhisattva’s clarity and precision, free from error or confusion.
Furthermore, it extinguishes immeasurable marks.
Through such skillful means, one is able to extinguish the views of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Through such skillful means, one is able to extinguish discursive thought.
Each possesses its own specific primary and auxiliary factors;
the Bodhisattva perceives them all with complete clarity, without the slightest error.
Furthermore, these very skillful means and their various primary and auxiliary aspects are all without variety;
yet, while there is no variety, one distinguishes them as varieties without error or confusion.
Moreover, such skillful means are able to analyze and extinguish the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*).
Furthermore, by such skillful means one can realize and extinguish the four abidings;
by such skillful means one can extinguish the sands of dust;
by such skillful means one can extinguish ignorance.
Although these various and manifold [teachings] are distinct and unmixed with one another,
they appear as many due to the distinctions made among the three *siddhāntas*;
however, in the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, there is no plurality.
Although there are not several [distinct categories], they are called "several" for the sake of discussion based on their multiplicity;
this refers to the immeasurable Four Noble Truths.
As for the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) Four Noble Truths:
All are the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and inconceivable.
It is not only that in the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) there are no longer any diversities;
even in the three *siddhāntas* and all phenomena, there are no longer any diversities.
This meaning can be understood and need not be recorded in further detail.
If one correlates the Four Noble Truths vertically with the various lands, there are increases and decreases.
In the Land of Common Residence, there are four [truths].
The provisional means consist of three;
the true reward consists of two;
and the land of tranquil light consists of only one.
If there are those who oppose one horizontally,
though they dwell together in arising and ceasing,
through skillful means one remains free from arising and ceasing.
The True Reward Land is immeasurable;
the Land of Peaceful Light is unconditioned, and so forth.
Furthermore, these are collectively termed the Four Noble Truths.
To speak of them separately, they are called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Suffering (*duḥkha*) consists of seven branches: consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Accumulation (*samudaya*) consists of five branches: ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).
The Path is the skillful means that serves as the counteractive cause and condition;
cessation is the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra opens forth the fourfold Four Noble Truths.
It also reveals the forty-two links of dependent origination:
by observing them with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
by observing them with middling wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Through the contemplation of superior wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a bodhisattva;
through the contemplation of the most superior wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a Buddha.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says:
Phenomena produced by causes and conditions are themselves subject to arising and ceasing;
I say that they are empty.
This is without arising or ceasing;
it is also called a provisional name;
it is immeasurable.
It is also called the meaning of the Middle Way;
it is non-action. Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:
Dependent origination is itself accumulation;
that which arises is itself suffering;
the means for extinguishing suffering is the path.
The exhaustion of the origin of suffering is cessation.
Furthermore, a verse says "causes and conditions";
causes and conditions are precisely ignorance.
The phenomena that arise are precisely the formations, name-and-form, the six sense bases, and so forth;
therefore, the text says:
"For disciples of sharp faculties, he taught the twelve links of dependent origination as having the characteristic of neither arising nor ceasing."
This refers to the preceding twenty-five chapters,
which explain the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination for disciples of dull faculties.
This refers to the final two chapters.
It should be understood that the verses of this treatise speak of four sets of the Four Noble Truths in their general sense,
and four sets of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination in their specific sense.
The detailed analysis of these four sets of the Four Noble Truths is now complete.
The various sutras clarify the manifold ways of generating the bodhicitta:
some state that one generates the bodhicitta by contemplating various principles,
while others state that one generates the bodhicitta upon beholding the various marks of the Buddha.
Some behold various supernormal powers;
some hear various teachings;
some travel through various lands.
Some behold various multitudes;
some see the cultivation of various practices;
some see the cessation of various dharmas.
Or one may see various faults, or see others undergoing various sufferings, and thereby generate the bodhicitta.
Briefly stated, ten such instances are primary; for a detailed explanation, and so forth.
Regarding those who resolve their minds through inference:
the nature of phenomena is such by its very nature that it cannot be defiled by accumulation nor afflicted by suffering.
The Path cannot lead to penetration, and cessation cannot bring about purity;
it is like clouds shrouding the moon, which cannot obstruct it.
Only after dispelling afflictions does one perceive the Dharma-nature.
The Sūtra says:
"Cessation is not the ultimate truth; it is because cessation accords with the ultimate that it is so designated.
Since even cessation is not the ultimate, how much less could the other three truths be?"
Within afflictions there is no bodhi; within bodhi there are no afflictions.
This is called the contemplation of the arising and ceasing of the Four Noble Truths, seeking the Buddha-way above and transforming sentient beings below, thereby giving rise to the bodhicitta.
Regarding those who resolve their minds by inferring the Four Truths through non-arising:
the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not distinct from suffering and its origin; it is only that, being deluded regarding suffering and its origin, one loses sight of the nature of phenomena.

Just as when water freezes it is still water and there is no separate water, so too, when one penetrates suffering and its origin, there is neither suffering nor its origin; this is precisely to realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Even suffering and its origin are [the nature of phenomena].
How much more so regarding the cessation of the Path!
As the Sūtra says:
"Afflictions are themselves bodhi."
Enlightenment is itself affliction;
this is called the aspiration for bodhicitta through the investigation of the Four Noble Truths as being unborn, seeking the higher while transforming those below.
Regarding the investigation of the immeasurable:
Now, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
It is not even within the realm of the two vehicles, let alone that of ordinary beings.
Apart from the manifestations of the two extremes, there exists a distinct pure dharma.
As stated in the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* in the section on the ten similes, and so forth;
this is called "seeking enlightenment by investigating the four truths of the immeasurable [realms] for the sake of upward seeking and downward transformation.
It is called "investigating the absence of an agent."
Indeed, the dharma-nature and all phenomena are non-dual and without distinction.
This is true even for ordinary dharmas,
let alone those of the two vehicles.
To seek the true reality apart from ordinary phenomena is like avoiding this emptiness and seeking emptiness elsewhere; thus,
ordinary phenomena themselves are the true reality.
There is no need to abandon the mundane to turn toward the sacred;
as the Sūtra says:
"Birth-and-death is itself Nirvāṇa."
A single form and a single fragrance are both the Middle Way.
This is called investigating the Uncreated Four Noble Truths to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below, thereby giving rise to the bodhicitta.
If one investigates even a single dharma, one will immediately penetrate the Dharma-realm, reaching its limits and its depths.
Only when one is ultimately endowed with both the horizontal and vertical, as well as phenomena and principle,
and possesses both the upward seeking of enlightenment and the downward transformation of beings within oneself,
can it truly be called the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Bodhi is called the Way (mārga).
Because the Way can lead one across to the far shore— both horizontally and vertically—
it is called the Perfection of Arousing the Mind (cittotpāda-pāramitā).
Therefore, in this process of inference, one must thoroughly investigate the phenomena and principles at both shallow and deep levels;
all subsequent dharmas are to be treated in this same manner.
*Mahā-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Mohe zhiguan), Fascicle One, Part One.
